Introduction

It is a black March. Having swept through Asia, COVID-19 is now raging across Europe. Countries are responding in different ways, and on the whole the results are worrying. I hope the pandemic ends soon and life gets back to normal as quickly as possible.

Europe’s handling of the pandemic can be exasperating at times, but in acoustics it has flourished for a century and leads the world. Many people have sent me private messages on Zhihu and WeChat asking about studying acoustics in Europe, so today let’s talk about some of Europe’s best-known universities and acoustics labs.

I’ll go country by country, listing the important university acoustics labs in each and then describing a few in more detail, mostly ones I have worked with or know reasonably well. My view is limited, so if I have got anything wrong or left out a university or lab, please do fill in the gaps.

Germany

  1. RWTH Aachen University

  2. Technical University of Berlin (TU Berlin)

  3. Technical University of Munich (TUM)

  4. University of Oldenburg

  5. Technical University of Braunschweig (TU Braunschweig)

  6. Leibniz University Hannover

Note: the universities in bold are the ones I describe in more detail. The same goes for the other countries.

1. RWTH Aachen University, Institute of Technical Acoustics (ITA)

https://www.akustik.rwth-aachen.de/www.akustik.rwth-aachen.de

My alma mater, so naturally it comes first. The institute is over fifty years old; I was there for its fiftieth anniversary while doing my PhD. It is well known in German and international acoustics. Its former director, Heinrich Kuttruff, and its current director (also my doctoral supervisor), Michael Vorländer, are both renowned German acousticians.

ITA started out in room acoustics. Kuttruff wrote the classics Acoustics and Room Acoustics. A few years ago, in his eighties, he was still driving to the institute every so often to look things up for the latest edition of Room Acoustics.

A history of acoustics: architectural acoustics

While writing my history of ultrasonics recently, I was surprised to find that Professor Kuttruff had also written a book on ultrasonics. I have to say, the old professor is not only remarkably energetic but impressively wide-ranging in his knowledge.

A history of acoustics: ultrasonics, and the search for Jack that began with the Titanic

Over the past ten-odd years the institute has expanded into virtual acoustics and auralization in a big way. Professor Vorländer’s Auralization, published in 2007, can be regarded as the classic text in the field.

A history of acoustics: auralization

In the 2010s Janina Fels became a professor there and started research in medical acoustics, which has been growing steadily ever since.

Once I start talking about my own institute I can’t stop, things get out of hand and the article threatens to wander off topic. Back to business: here are the institute’s main research areas.

Room acoustics: simulation based on geometrical acoustics, and real-time simulation of sound transmission between multiple rooms.

Environmental acoustics: auralization of urban environments and aircraft noise. This could really be merged with virtual acoustics below. The urban work is mainly for auralization too, with a focus on real-time simulation of diffraction. That project has been running for many years; the guy working on it has been at it for over six years without graduating, and I suspect he’s about to leave without a degree…

Virtual acoustics: modeling of moving sound sources (my own topic), 3D sound reproduction and real-time auralization. In fact, the room and environmental acoustics projects above are basically all tied in with virtual acoustics.

Medical acoustics: binaural hearing, individualized HRTFs and fast HRTF measurement, psychoacoustics, and hearing research combined with virtual acoustics.

Other: transfer path analysis (TPA) for electric vehicles, ultrasonics and more.

RWTH Aachen’s aixCAVE, a five-sided virtual reality environment; ITA handles the virtual acoustics [2]

ITA’s mobile hearing lab. Want to run listening tests with a particular group of people somewhere? Just drive there [1]

2. TU Berlin, Audio Communication Group

www.ak.tu-berlin.de

HRTF measurement

A long-established technical university with a long-established acoustics lab. It has worked with Aachen on room acoustics, running a round robin combined with virtual acoustics (look it up if you’re interested). The lab focuses on music and speech in acoustic and electroacoustic systems, including electroacoustic measurement, recording and reproduction technology, 3D virtual audio, binaural technology, sound field synthesis and the study of musical content in the media.

Anyone working on HRTFs will know their FABIAN database [3]. They have also studied the relationship between musical performance and room acoustics, using auralization and binaural playback to examine how performers are influenced by the rooms they play in [4].

3. Technical University of Munich

www.ei.tum.de

I very nearly (I couldn’t tell you how near) did my PhD here, under Bernhard U. Seeber. Professor Seeber was a student of Hugo Fastl, co-author of the bible of psychoacoustics, Psychoacoustics. And speaking of psychoacoustics, here come my humble efforts again ↓↓. It may look like a sneaky plug, but it’s all my own stuff, and it’s knowledge (knowledge, folks!), so my conscience is clear.

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 1

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 2

Professor Seeber’s group is called the Audio Information Processing Group (AIP). When I met him in Munich he had only just become a professor, and he was visibly riding high. Years later, chatting with my officemate in Aachen, I found out that he had been in touch with the same professor at almost the same time, and for various reasons hadn’t gone to Munich either. We sighed that in some parallel universe we might be officemates in Munich, wondering why we never went to Aachen!

German psychoacoustics has its roots in Munich, so psychoacoustics is still one of AIP’s strengths. Another focus is research on hearing aids and cochlear implants, including using virtual acoustics to study how the placement of hearing aid microphones affects the perception of sound sources.

Real-time processing for novel hearing aid algorithms. Sound signals are picked up with microphones in hearing aid shells, processed in a software hearing aid in Simulink on a laptop, and played by receivers in the ear canal – all in 7 ms. [5] Sound coding in a cochlear implant [5]

AIP is not the only group in Munich doing acoustics. In structural mechanics, Professor Gerhard Müller works on vibroacoustics; rumor has it he is the son of the founder of the engineering firm Müller-BBM. The acoustics side of his group mainly works on room acoustics, acoustic metamaterials and the like.

www.lnm.mw.tum.de

Another professor working in acoustics is Steffen Marburg, who specializes in numerical methods and computational acoustics.

www.professoren.tum.de

4. University of Oldenburg

www.uol.de

Unsurprisingly, many people have never heard of it: this is a university whose acoustics is better known than the university itself. In acoustics research related to people, Oldenburg is outstanding. The group focuses on auditory perception, psychoacoustics, virtual acoustics, sound quality and the associated digital signal processing algorithms, sound reproduction systems and more.

The first academic conference of my PhD was in Oldenburg, which makes it unforgettable. Apart from the excitement, I remember that almost every presentation was in German. For someone who was then a total beginner in German, that was a heavy blow, and it set off my mad rush to learn the language.

On the banks of the Hunte in Oldenburg, taken when I sneaked out during the conference

United Kingdom

  1. University of Southampton

  2. University of Salford

  3. University College London (UCL)

  4. University of Liverpool

  5. University of York

  6. University of Edinburgh

1. University of Southampton, Institute of Sound and Vibration Research (ISVR)

www.southampton.ac.uk

Where my current boss studied.

By headcount, it is probably the largest acoustics lab in the world.

Its main research areas include noise control, transportation noise, vibration and noise, underwater acoustics, ultrasonics, audio engineering and sound perception. ISVR covers an enormous range of topics and works with many companies.

A multichannel loudspeaker array

If you want to understand the principles of acoustics, don’t miss ISVR’s acoustics animations! I have used them many times in my lecture slides and articles. They are simple, clear and memorable.

http://resource.isvr.soton.ac.uk/spcg/tutorial/tutorial/Tutorial_files/Web-basics-nature.htmresource.isvr.soton.ac.uk

2. University of Salford

www.salford.ac.uk

Another classic case of acoustics being more famous than its university. Professor Trevor Cox is a star of acoustics outreach and a role model of mine. He works closely with the BBC and has appeared on screen many times.

The acoustics group focuses on architectural acoustics, audio engineering, environmental noise, acoustic materials, psychoacoustics and more.

3. UCL

www.ucl.ac.uk

Home of the architectural acoustics group of Jian Kang, a leading Chinese acoustician. The group works mainly on soundscapes, covering environmental and architectural acoustics.

4. University of Liverpool, Acoustics Research Unit (ARU)

https://www.liverpool.ac.uk/architecture/research/acoustics-research-unit/about/www.liverpool.ac.uk

One of the partner universities in a project I used to work on; I spent a week at a summer school there.

Professor Carl Hopkins works mainly on vibration and noise and has done in-depth research on structure-borne sound. There is also a Korean lecturer working on psychoacoustics and soundscapes, who recently took an interest in my PhD topic, moving source modeling, possibly for soundscape listening tests. I hope we can work together.

Denmark

  1. Technical University of Denmark (DTU)

  2. Aalborg University

1. Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Acoustic Technology (ACT)

http://www.act.elektro.dtu.dk/www.act.elektro.dtu.dk

One of the largest acoustics institutes in Europe. Its research falls into four main areas:

Sound field analysis and measurement

Electroacoustics and transducer technology

Structure-borne sound

Architectural acoustics

During my PhD, ACT came to Aachen for an academic exchange. I still remember the admiring little glances from my male colleagues in the audience when a French woman PhD student gave her talk →_→.

The late Professor Finn Jacobsen had deep ties with the company I work for now. They collaborated for more than twenty years, until his sad passing a few years ago. His Fundamentals of General Linear Acoustics was the first acoustics book I ever bought, and I still leaf through it often.

Thanks to its location, ACT works extensively with the acoustic transducer giant B&K and with the hearing aid companies Oticon, Widex, GN ReSound and others.

France

First, a gripe: it is really hard to find information on French university websites, and the sites themselves are very odd. Maybe that’s because I don’t speak French…

  1. Le Mans University

  2. Sorbonne University

  3. Aix-Marseille University

1. Le Mans University

www.lemans-acoustique.fr

laum.univ-lemans.fr

The lab is divided into three groups: materials, transducers and structures. What little I know is that they do a lot of work on acoustic metamaterials and publish a great deal. I just had a look, and the materials group is huge, with seven professors alone, so no wonder it is so productive.

2. Sorbonne University

www.dalembert.upmc.fr

I don’t know this group well. I had a little contact with Professor Brian Katz when I was helping my professor write a proposal. Katz started out in HRTFs and now works mainly on virtual acoustics, auralization, room acoustics and spatial hearing. He is a rigorous scholar and gave us lots of very useful (critical) comments on our proposal -_-.

Belgium

  1. KU Leuven

  2. Ghent University

KU Leuven

www.mech.kuleuven.be

Another big acoustics group: Professor Wim Desmet leads several dozen people.

The research leans toward vibration and structures; on the acoustics side it covers vibroacoustics, aeroacoustic noise, acoustic metamaterials and more.

A 3D-printed acoustic metamaterial I photographed when I visited their acoustics lab in 2018

The Netherlands

Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e)

https://www.tue.nl/en/research/research-groups/building-acoustics/

I spent a year in TU/e’s building acoustics group. Its head, Maarten Hornikx, was promoted to associate professor only last year and is vice dean of the Department of the Built Environment: young, accomplished and on a smooth career path.

Under his leadership the group keeps growing. Since he took it over in 2012, it has become a large group of more than a dozen people. Its main research areas are building acoustics and computational acoustics, the craft Maarten built his career on. In recent years it has gradually branched out into auralization, acoustic metamaterials and sound perception, with some success.

The Nordic countries

  1. Finland: Aalto University

  2. Sweden: Chalmers University of Technology

  3. Norway: Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)

1. Aalto University

www.aalto.fi

Another large acoustics group, bringing together labs from three fields: signal processing and acoustics, computer science, and media. So its research is very broad, including audio signal processing, communication acoustics, concert hall acoustics, room acoustics modeling, sound and music computing, and virtual acoustics.

At the start of this year I was in Finland on a business trip (and, courtesy of my Finnish colleagues, caught a nasty flu; for a while I wondered whether it was COVID…). I paid a short visit to the Aalto acoustics lab. Their facilities are excellent, with every kind of lab you could want, and I toured their newly renovated anechoic chamber.

Incidentally, Tapio Lokki was one of the first researchers to work on auralization and virtual acoustics; he and Professor Vorländer can both be called founders of auralization.

The quietest place in Finland isn’t Santa Claus Village; it’s this ↑

2. Chalmers University of Technology

www.ta.chalmers.se

Applied acoustics at Chalmers is split into two groups: the vibration and noise group led by the veteran professor Wolfgang Kropp, and the audio technology group led by Jens Ahrens. That’s right, it’s a German-run outfit. Professor Kropp came to Gothenburg decades ago to take over the group and is known for his work on tire noise. Beyond that, the vibration group focuses on active control of vibration and noise, outdoor sound propagation, and sound and vibration quality, while the audio group works on 3D sound capture and reproduction, and microphone and loudspeaker arrays.

I have been there three times: once to wander around with a PhD student I knew, and twice for summer schools. What struck me most was how good the coffee was, and that there was often free fruit. Truly socialist perks.

Summary

The founding fathers of acoustics, Helmholtz and Rayleigh, were a German and an Englishman, so it is no exaggeration to say that acoustics was born in Europe. Its leading universities have long traditions of acoustics research, attracting countless students and active collaboration from industry.

Again, my knowledge is limited, so I can’t guarantee that every group is described completely or entirely correctly. Additions and corrections are very welcome!
